_meta.note: Apple platforms have two kinds of material: Liquid Glass (the functional layer: controls and navigation) and standard materials (the content layer). Apple's guidance is qualitative except where tagged apple-hig. The numeric blur/layer budgets are NOT Apple numbers: they come from independent accessibility audits and Figma's Glass effect, are tagged per rule, and are guardrails to confirm, not gospel.
_meta.verify_against: HIG > Foundations > Materials; WWDC25 'Meet Liquid Glass'; SwiftUI 'Applying Liquid Glass to custom views'; current Xcode SDK
_meta.checked: 2026-10-17 against the live HIG Materials page (last changed 2025-09-09) and the SwiftUI docs for OS 26 and the OS 27 betas

system_materials.ios_ipados: The HIG names four standard materials for the content layer: ultra-thin, thin, regular (default), thick. SwiftUI also offers .ultraThickMaterial and .bar (matches system toolbars). UIKit: UIBlurEffect.Style (.systemUltraThinMaterial ... .systemChromeMaterial).
system_materials.macos: macOS materials have designated purposes (sidebar, menu, popover, headerView, windowBackground...): use NSVisualEffectView.Material by purpose, with a behind-window or within-window blending mode.
system_materials.guidance: Pick a material by meaning and use, not by the color it seems to give. Thicker = more opaque = better contrast for text and fine detail; thinner = more context shows through. Put vibrant colors (label, secondaryLabel, fill, separator vibrancy) on top; avoid quaternary label vibrancy on thin and ultraThin.

apple_guidance.rule: Liquid Glass is the functional layer for controls and navigation (tab bars, toolbars, sidebars, sheets) that floats above content. Don't use it in the content layer; use standard materials there. Exception: transient interactive controls in the content layer, like sliders and toggles. System components adopt it automatically; apply it to custom controls sparingly, only for the most important functional elements. Apple publishes NO numeric blur-radius cap or layer count.

variants.regular: Default (Glass.regular). Blurs and adjusts the luminosity of what is behind it to keep text legible. Use it for most components, and always for text-heavy ones: alerts, sidebars, popovers.
variants.clear: Glass.clear. Highly translucent. Only for components that float over visually rich backgrounds such as photos and video. Needs a dimming layer when the content behind is bright (see clear_dimming).
variants.identity: Glass.identity. No effect: use it to switch glass off conditionally without changing the view tree.
variants.user_settings: The look can change with system settings: the person's preferred Liquid Glass look, Reduce Transparency, Increase Contrast. Test with all of them.

clear_dimming.rule: Over bright content, add a dark dimming layer of about 35% opacity behind clear glass. Over dark enough content, or with AVKit's standard playback controls (they bring their own dimming), skip it.

control_depth_max.note: Figma Glass 'Depth' >20 harms readability for UI controls

frost_range.note: Figma Glass 'Frost'; >30 reads as milky plastic

min_text_contrast.when: measured AFTER blur against the actual backdrop

over_photo.rule: Over a photo or video: for floating controls, use clear glass plus the 35% dimming layer when the image is bright (clear_dimming). For text-heavy panels, use regular glass, or a standard material in the content layer (.thickMaterial / .ultraThickMaterial), or a legibility scrim (a gradient from .clear to a semantic background over the text band). Re-measure contrast AFTER blur either way; never rely on glass alone for legibility over imagery.

fallback.rule: System glass adapts by itself. For custom effects, ship a solid (or near-solid) variant and swap at runtime (SwiftUI: @Environment(\.accessibilityReduceTransparency)). Never rely on translucency for legibility.

lift_tip.note: Keep text/symbols on a layer ABOVE the glass group; a subtle inner light (white ~30%, blur ~6) helps separation.
